title: Chapter 65: Breathing the Dead, Part 3 of 5: Making Ready
html:
The sun went down behind the hills in the west like a coal dropped into water, quick and red, and the cold came down after it all at once.
Lyra had never felt cold come so fast. In the city the cold crept in, in the evening, slowly, through the cracks in the windows and under the doors, and you had time to put on another shawl. Here it fell. One moment the low gold light was lying across the camp and she could feel a little warmth on her face from it. The next the light was gone, and the sky over the hills was a hard clear green, and the breath was smoking out of her mouth, and her fingers in her gloves were aching.
And behind her, over the ridge, the pale light of the Glass rose up into the dark like milk poured into ink.
The camp lit the big fire.
They did it all together. That was the first thing she noticed. Nobody was told to come, and nobody stayed away. They came out of the tents as the light went, every one of them, the old ones on their sticks and the children in their capes and the mothers with their babies, and they stood round the great heap of thorn wood in the middle of the camp, the heap that had been growing all day, and waited. And Kestrel came out of the gray tent with a brand from her own fire in her hand, a long stick with flame on the end of it, and walked once all the way round the heap, slowly, in the direction the sun goes. And then she stopped on the south side of it, with her back to the camp and her face to the ridge and the Glass, and pushed the brand into the bottom of the heap.
The thorn was very dry. It went up at once. Not slowly, the way a fire starts in a grate. All at once, with a great soft roar, like a breath let out, and the flames went up higher than a man, higher than two men, yellow and orange and full of sparks. The heat came out of it in a wave that made Lyra step back. The faces round the ring lit up orange. The handprints on the tents nearest the fire lit up and seemed to move.
And then the women came with the bowls.
Wooden bowls, wide and shallow, each one carried in both hands. In each bowl there was a heap of the brown dry herb that they had been grinding all day in the stone bowls outside the tents. The women walked round the fire, one after another, and each one, as she passed the south side, threw a handful of the herb into the flames.
The smoke changed.
It went thick and slow and pale, almost white, and it did not go straight up the way woodsmoke does. It hung. It spread out low over the ground in the still cold air, in a soft drifting layer, waist-high, and it smelled of burnt honey so strongly that Lyra could taste it on her tongue and feel it in the back of her throat, sweet and dark and a little bitter. It made her eyes water. It made her head feel light, a little, the way a glass of wine does on an empty stomach.
"Don't breathe too deep," said a voice beside her. "Not yet. It's not for you."
It was Arran. He had put his tunic and his fur back on, and his hair was wet, as if he had washed. He was not grinning now. His face was quiet and serious in the firelight, and there was a fresh line of gray painted down it, over the old one, very neat.
"What does it do?" said Lyra.
"Makes it easier," said Arran. "For the ones who breathe. It opens you up. Like warm water opens up your hands when they're stiff." He looked at the fire. "And it makes it easier for the one who's giving. It loosens what's in them. So it comes out soft. Not torn."
All round the fire, people were painting their faces.
There were pots of it. Little clay pots, the ones the children had been carrying about all day, full of a thick gray paste. Ash, Lyra thought, and water, and something to make it stick. People dipped two fingers in and drew a line down their own faces, forehead to nose, slowly. Or they did it for each other. A mother for a child. A young man for an old woman whose hands shook too much. Even the ones whose faces were already gray, the old man with the gray cheeks and the woman with the gray down her throat, even they painted a fresh line, over the gray that was already there, so that every face round the fire had the line on it, new and wet and shining in the firelight.
A child came up to Lyra with a pot.
It was the girl. The serious one from the path, the biggest of the three who had said stop. She stood in front of Lyra with the pot held out in both hands and looked up at her, very solemnly, and did not say anything.
Lyra looked at Arran.
"You don't have to," said Arran. "You're not breathing tonight. But she's asking."
Lyra looked down at the girl. At the small round shaved head, and the gray line already painted on it, a little crooked, and the dark serious eyes.
She knelt down on the gravel so that her face was level with the girl's.
The girl dipped two fingers in the pot. Her fingers were very small and very cold. She put them on Lyra's forehead, at the top, just under the edge of the red scarf. And drew them down. Slowly. Carefully. Her tongue between her teeth with the effort of keeping it straight. Down between Lyra's eyebrows. Down the bridge of her nose. Down to the tip.
The paste was cold and gritty and smelled of smoke.
The girl took her fingers away and looked at what she had done, frowning a little. Then she nodded, satisfied, and turned and went away with her pot, and did not look back.
Lyra stayed kneeling.
She put her gloved hand up, very carefully, and touched the line on her own face with one fingertip. It was already beginning to dry.
When she stood up, the ring had changed.
The crowd had drawn back from the fire. Not far. A few steps. Enough to leave a wide circle of bare beaten earth all round the blaze, lit orange, with the low white smoke drifting over it. And on the south side of the fire, in the circle, between the fire and the ridge, the grass mats had been laid out. A ring of them. Small, round, close together.
Twelve of them.
And on each mat, as she watched, someone came and sat down.
They came out of the crowd one by one, without any sign that she could see, as if they had always known who it would be. An old woman with a gray chin. A young man with the bone beads in his hair. The wide woman from the bread stones, who looked across the fire at Lyra and nodded to her once. A thin gray-bearded man with only one arm. A girl not much older than Lyra herself, with a baby, who handed the baby to someone in the crowd before she sat. Others. Men and women, old and young. Each of them sat down cross-legged on a mat, facing inward, toward the empty middle of the ring, with their hands on their knees.
Kestrel was the eleventh.
And the twelfth was Old Hask.
The boy led him. The same small boy as last night, walking in front, with the old man's hand on his shoulder. Hask was humming. Round and round, up a little and down a little, the same shapeless tune. He did not seem to need the boy. He walked straight to the last empty mat, and the boy and Kestrel let him down onto it between them, slowly, the way they had last night, with his knees cracking, and he sat there in the firelight with his white blind eyes and his gray face and his little beard plaits shining, and went on humming.
There was one mat left in the middle. In the very center of the ring. Bigger than the others.
Empty.
Lyra looked at it. And then she looked round for Corin.
He was standing on the other side of the fire, at the edge of the crowd, with Oren close behind him. He was looking at the empty mat too. His face in the orange light was very pale.
And then Kestrel stood up from her mat, and turned, and looked across the ring at him, and held out one long hand.
She did not say anything. She did not have to.
Outside the Ring
Corin went.
Lyra watched him do it. He gave his crutch to Oren without looking at him, and Oren took it without a word, and Corin walked out across the bare earth toward the ring of mats on his own, limping. It was not far. Twenty steps, perhaps. But it seemed to take him a long time. The white smoke drifted round his knees. The firelight moved on his back. Every face in the crowd turned to follow him, and nobody said anything, and the only sounds were the roar of the fire and the hum of the Glass and the soft scrape of his bad foot on the gravel.
He stepped between two of the mats, careful not to touch them, into the ring.
And stopped by the empty mat in the middle, and looked down at it.
Kestrel had come in after him. She stood in front of him and said something, too low for Lyra to hear. He nodded. Then, slowly, awkwardly, with his bad leg stuck out stiff in front of him, he got down onto the mat and sat. Cross-legged, as far as he could. His hands on his knees. Facing north. Facing the ridge and the milky light and the Glass beyond.
The twelve sat round him in their ring, facing in, with the firelight on their shoulders.
Kestrel looked down at him for a moment. Then she turned and came back out of the ring, stepping between the mats the way he had, and came straight across the bare earth to where Lyra stood at the front of the crowd.
"You," she said.
Lyra's heart turned over.
"Come," said Kestrel.
She led her round the outside of the ring. Not into it. Round it, behind the backs of the twelve, past the old woman with the gray chin and the young man with the beads and the one-armed man, to the north side. The side between the ring and the ridge. The side Corin was facing. There was a place there, just outside the ring, between two of the mats, a little gap in the circle where you could see straight in, past the shoulders of the twelve, to the mat in the middle and the man sitting on it.
There was a stone there. A flat round gray stone, set into the ground, worn smooth and hollow in the top, the way a step is worn by feet.
"Sit," said Kestrel.
Lyra sat on the stone. It was cold through her coat.
From here she could see Corin's face. He was looking straight at her, across the ring, past the twelve, his face lit orange by the fire behind the twelve and pale under the orange. She did not know if he could see her. The fire was behind her, too, behind the twelve on the far side, but the smoke was between them, and the light came and went.
Kestrel crouched down beside the stone. Close. Her mouth near Lyra's ear.
"Listen to us," she said. Very low. "This is your place. Someone always sits in it. Someone who is not breathing. Someone who knows the one in the middle. Who knows his name." She paused. "Not his name on papers. His name. The one you would call across a street."
Lyra nodded. Her mouth had gone dry.
"When we begin," said Kestrel, "he will go down. Into himself. The way he goes down when he takes. He knows how. He has done it more times than any of us." Her voice was very steady. "But this is not taking. This is the other way. He will be letting go. And when a man who has spent his whole life holding on begins to let go, sometimes he does not know where to stop."
Lyra stared at her.
"Sometimes," said Kestrel, "they let go of too much. They give away the woman they carry, and then they keep going. They give away the next one. And the next. And then they give away themselves. They go down so far that they do not come back up. They are still sitting there on the mat, breathing. But nobody is inside."
The fire roared. The smoke drifted.
"You will know," said Kestrel. "You will see it in his face. You will feel it, here." She touched Lyra's chest, once, lightly, with two fingers, over her heart. "If you see him going too far, you say his name. Say it loud. Say it the way you would say it if you saw him walking off a roof." Her eyes in the firelight were very dark. "And he will hear it, and he will know where up is. That is what you are for."
"And if he doesn't hear it?"
Kestrel was quiet for a moment.
"Then you say it again," she said.
She stood up.
"Do not come into the ring," she said. "Whatever you see. Do not cross the mats. Do not touch him. Only his name. If you come in, you will be breathing too, and you do not know how, and the smoke will open you, and then we will have two to bring back instead of one." She looked down at Lyra. "Do you understand us?"
"Yes," said Lyra.
"Say it."
"I stay here. I don't go in. I don't touch him. If he goes too far, I say his name."
"Good."
Kestrel turned to go. Then she stopped, and looked back over her shoulder.
"Do you know it?" she said. "His name? The one you would call?"
Lyra opened her mouth to say yes, of course. Corin. Everybody knew his name. It was on the posters in the city. It was in the Ledger in his own crooked hand on the first page. It was not a hard name.
And then she stopped.
Because that was not what Kestrel was asking.
She thought of all the things she had called him. In all the days since he had stopped knowing her. She had called him harvester, when she was angry, which was often. She had called him Vane, once or twice, in the cold voice she used on servants who had broken something. She had called him you, mostly. Hey. Listen. Look at me. She had called him a fool and an idiot and a liar, and once, on the roof garden, a word she would not have said in front of her mother.
And then there was the other name. The one she did not say. The one she had said, a long time ago, when he still knew who she was. That was gone. She had decided it was gone, the night she found out what he had burned.
She looked across the ring at him, sitting on his mat in the smoke, with his gray hands on his knees, waiting.
"Yes," she said. "I know it."
Kestrel looked at her a moment longer. Then she nodded, and went back round the ring, and stepped in between the mats, and sat down on her own mat in the circle, the eleventh, beside Old Hask.
Lyra sat on the cold stone.
Someone came and stood behind her. She did not have to look round. She knew the shape of him by the way the firelight changed on the ground. Big, and steady, and smelling of sweat and woodsmoke and the goat that had followed him all day.
Oren put his hand on her shoulder. Once. The way he did every night before he slept. And then took it away again, and stood behind her, with his arms folded and Corin's crutch leaning against his leg, and said nothing.
In the ring, Old Hask stopped humming.
And the whole camp went still.
The Rite
Kestrel got up from her mat and went to him.
She knelt in front of him, in the middle of the ring, close, so that her knees were almost touching his. And she reached out with both hands and took hold of the collar of his coat.
Lyra's hands closed on her knees.
Kestrel unbuttoned the coat. Slowly. One button, and the next, and the next, down to his chest. Then she opened the collar of the shirt under it, the old gray shirt from Silas's crypt, and folded it back, so that his throat was bare, and the top of his chest, and the line of his collarbones. The skin there was pale and ordinary, the skin of a man who had not been in the sun all winter. The gray did not show. Lyra knew where it was. Under his sleeves, a hand's width below each shoulder, less a finger, where it stopped in a line like the edge of a tide. But here, at his throat, there was only skin.
Kestrel looked at his left shoulder for a moment anyway, as if she could see through the cloth to the line. She did not touch it.
Then she put her hands flat on his shoulders, one on each side, on the bare skin at the base of his neck, and leaned in, and said something to him. Lyra could not hear it. She saw Corin's lips move in answer. Then she saw him shut his eyes.
Kestrel took her hands away and went back to her mat and sat down.
And the twelve began to breathe.
They did it together. All twelve of them, at once, as if someone had given a sign, though Lyra had seen no sign. They leaned in. Toward the middle. Toward him. Not far. Only a little, from where they sat, bending forward from the waist with their hands still on their knees, so that their twelve faces came a little closer to him, all round, in a ring. And they breathed in.
Slowly.
Lyra heard it. Twelve breaths, drawn in at once, long and slow and deep, through the nose. It was a soft sound. Like wind going into a cave. It went on for a long time. Longer than Lyra could have breathed in, herself. She found she was holding her own breath while she listened to it.
Then they breathed out. Slowly. Away from him. Turning their heads a little to the side, each of them, so that the breath went out into the smoke and not back toward the middle.
And in again.
And out.
And in.
The fire roared on the south side of the ring. The white smoke drifted low over the ground, and where it drifted into the ring it seemed to slow, and thicken, and hang round the twelve, so that they sat in a soft pale haze, and the firelight came through it orange and dim. The hum of the Glass came up through the stone Lyra sat on, into her bones. Nobody in the crowd moved. Nobody spoke. A baby began to cry somewhere and was hushed at once.
And Corin sat in the middle with his eyes shut and his coat open and his gray hands on his knees, and did not move at all.
Lyra watched his face.
For a long time nothing happened. The twelve breathed, in and out, in and out, and his face did not change. It was very still and very pale, the way it went when he was harvesting, the way she had seen it go before, in the city, when he took. Gone inward. Gone down. The eyes moving a little under the lids, the way eyes move in sleep.
Then something rose off his shoulders.
At first Lyra thought it was the smoke. It was so faint. A thin gray haze, lifting off the bare skin of his neck and his collarbones, very slowly, the way mist lifts off a pond in the morning. But it was not white, like the smoke. It was gray. A soft pale ash-gray, like breath on a cold window. And it did not drift away south with the smoke. It went up, a little. And then it went out. Toward the twelve. Toward their leaning faces, in thin slow threads, twelve of them, like the spokes of a wheel. Drawn out of him and into them by their breath.
Lyra's nails dug into her knees through her gloves.
And then she saw the pictures.
She did not see them with her eyes. Or she did, and she did not. They were in the gray. In the threads of mist going out from his shoulders. Faint, and quick, and gone almost as soon as they came, the way pictures come in the coals of a fire when you stare at them too long. But she saw them. She knew she did.
A wet stone. Gray, slick, by black water. And a small red hand on it, and a knife. A knife too big for the hand. And silver fish, a pile of them, shining. And cold. She did not see the cold. But she felt it, all at once, in her own small hands, for a breath. Then it was gone, into the thread that went to the old woman with the gray chin, and the old woman's face moved, very slightly, the mouth going tight, as if she had tasted something bitter.
A dark place behind stacked crates, and the smell of the harbor, and a boy's face very close. A laughing boy with yellow hair. Gone into the young man with the beads.
A garden. A garden under glass. A long room made all of glass, with the winter outside and the light coming through gray, and inside, trees in tubs. Small trees with dark shining leaves, and on the trees, oranges. Bright as lamps. Dozens of them. A whole glass room full of small orange suns. Gone into the wide woman from the bread stones, and the wide woman's eyes opened a little, in the haze, and filled with tears, and shut again.
A ballroom. Enormous. Chandeliers. A floor like black water. And an old, old man in a coat covered in gold lace bending down, very low, bowing to a little girl in a borrowed dress, and the room laughing. And the little girl not laughing. The little girl standing very straight, with her chin up, and her face burning, and something hard and cold starting in her chest that would never melt. Gone into the one-armed man.
A small glass jar held up to a lamp. A woman's gloved hand reaching for it. Four silver coins on a table. Gone into the girl who had given her baby away to sit in the ring.
More. Faster now. Too fast to see. A spade going into frozen earth. A cellar being dug. Bricks. Ice. Rows of little beds. Lyra flinched from that one and it was gone before she could see more. Jars on shelves. Hundreds. Glowing. A black lace fan. A violet gown. A necklace of tiny lights on a black chain. A mirror.
The threads went out and out, into the twelve. And the twelve breathed, and breathed, and the pictures went into them, one after another, a little into each, so that none of them took too much. And their faces moved as the pictures went in. Small movements. A frown. A softening. A mouth that went up at one corner, or down. As if they were each, for a moment, someone else.
And Corin's face changed too.
As the gray went out of him, his face got lighter. Not paler. Lighter. The way a man's face looks when he puts down a heavy load he has been carrying a long way. The lines round his eyes eased. His mouth, which had been shut hard, came a little open. His shoulders, which had been up round his ears since the fens, came down. A little. And a little more.
Lyra watched it, and could not breathe.
It was working. Whatever it was. It was working.
And then the threads slowed.
The gray mist off his shoulders was thinner now. Much thinner. Only a faint haze, hardly there. The pictures in it had stopped. The twelve were still breathing, in and out, but slower, and there was nothing much going into them anymore. Only a little gray, here and there, in wisps.
It was nearly done.
Lyra let out her breath.
And then, from deep in the middle of him, from somewhere far down under everything, something else began to rise.
It was not gray.
It was black.
